items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — the Governor is appointed by the Central Government and draws power from the RBI Act; the direction-issuing power is statutory, not constitutional
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the RBI Governor is appointed by the Central Government under Section 8 of the RBI Act, 1934. Statement 3 is correct for the same reason — the office and its powers are creatures of that Act, not of the Constitution. Statement 2 is the error: the Constitution of India contains no provision at all dealing with the RBI; the Centre's power to issue directions to the Bank 'in the public interest' comes from Section 7 of the RBI Act. Since statement 2 fails, options A, B and D are all excluded.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — casual workers fall within the EPF definition of 'employee', and the government may notify establishments that must pay wages only through a bank account; 'regular working hours' is not an entitlement of casual work
items.reasoning: Statement 3 is clearly correct: the proviso to Section 6 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (as amended in 2017, and carried into the Code on Wages, 2019) lets the appropriate Government notify industrial or other establishments whose employer must pay wages only by cheque or by crediting a bank account. Statement 1 is correct because the EPF & MP Act defines 'employee' as any person employed for wages in any kind of work in or in connection with the work of a covered establishment — the Act draws no line between permanent, temporary and casual employees, so casual workers are covered. Statement 2 fails: casual employment is by its nature irregular, and no law confers 'regular working hours' on casual workers as a class; hours-and-overtime protection flows from a specific statute such as the Factories Act to workers in covered establishments, not from casual status. The judgement call is on statement 2, hence MED rather than HIGH.

items.value: Increase in expenditure on public projects
items.reasoning: A recession is a demand deficiency, so the standard response is expansionary — pump money into the economy. Raising public project spending does exactly that and is unambiguously expansionary. Option D (cutting such spending) is contractionary and would deepen the slump, as would option C's tax increase. Option A pairs an expansionary tax cut with a contractionary rise in interest rates, so it works against itself and cannot be the step 'most likely' to be taken.

items.value: Statements 1 and 4 only — a costlier substitute raises demand, and a fall in the good's own price raises the quantity bought
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: when a substitute becomes dearer, buyers switch to this good and its demand curve shifts right. Statement 2 is wrong — a complement is consumed alongside the good, so a rise in the complement's price reduces demand for both. Statement 3 is wrong by the definition of an inferior good: demand for it falls as consumer income rises. Statement 4 is correct in the sense the question uses it — a lower own price raises the amount bought (strictly a movement along the demand curve rather than a shift). With 2 and 3 both false, only option A survives.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 only — UCBs may issue equity and preference shares, and were brought under the Banking Regulation Act in 1966; they are not regulated by State-created local boards
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is false and decides the question: urban cooperative banks are dual-regulated — the RBI for banking functions and the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies for incorporation and management — but there is no system of 'local boards set up by the State Governments' supervising them. Because statement 1 appears in options A, C and D, its falsity leaves only B. That reading is confirmed by the other two: UCBs were brought within the purview of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 by the 1966 amendment extending the Act to cooperative societies (statement 3), and they can raise capital by issuing equity and preference shares to members (statement 2).

items.value: All three — US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions, and inflation and short-term interest rates all influence Indian G-sec yields
items.reasoning: Yields are the market price of government borrowing and respond to every factor that moves the demand for and supply of that debt. The RBI sets the policy rate and conducts open market operations, so (2) is direct. Inflation erodes the real return on a fixed coupon and short-term rates anchor the near end of the yield curve, so (3) is direct. Fed decisions move global capital flows and the rupee-dollar interest differential, so foreign portfolio demand for Indian bonds — and hence their yields — shifts with them; (1) is therefore also correct.

items.value: Foreign currency convertible bonds, foreign institutional investment subject to conditions, and global depository receipts — but not NRE deposits
items.reasoning: FCCBs and GDRs are instruments through which a foreign investor takes an equity interest in an Indian company, and both are counted within India's FDI statistics. Foreign portfolio/institutional investment is ordinarily distinct from FDI, but crosses over 'with certain conditions' — an investment that takes a single foreign investor to 10 per cent or more of a company's paid-up capital is reclassified as FDI, which is exactly the qualification statement 2 carries. Non-resident external deposits are bank deposits by NRIs; they are recorded under banking capital in the capital account and are never treated as direct investment, so item 4 is excluded and only option A fits.

items.value: Statement 1 only — devaluation necessarily makes exports cheaper abroad, but does not raise the currency's external value and need not improve the trade balance
items.reasoning: Devaluation lowers the foreign-currency price of domestic goods, so statement 1 follows necessarily. Statement 2 is the opposite of what devaluation means — it reduces, not increases, the foreign value of the domestic currency. Statement 3 fails on the word 'necessarily': the trade balance improves only if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds (export and import demand elasticities summing above one), and in the short run the J-curve effect typically worsens the balance first because import bills rise before export volumes respond.

items.value: Loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion
items.reasoning: Black money is by definition income on which tax has not been paid, so its first and most direct effect on the State is a shortfall in revenue — which constrains every public programme the government funds. The other options describe real consequences of black money but they are downstream effects on the economy and polity rather than the government's own primary concern: diversion into real estate (A) and into gold and unproductive assets (B) are distortions of investment, and political funding and regionalism (C) is a political consequence, not a fiscal one. Marked MED because 'main cause of worry' calls for a judgement of emphasis rather than a fact stated in the stem.

items.value: Creation of new money to finance a budget deficit
items.reasoning: Printing fresh money — deficit financing or monetisation — adds to the money supply without any matching increase in output, which is the textbook cause of inflation. Borrowing from the public (B) merely transfers existing purchasing power from savers to the government, and repayment of public debt (A) is if anything anti-inflationary in its immediate effect. Borrowing from banks (C) is inflationary to a degree because it can expand credit, but it is bounded by existing bank resources and reserve requirements, so it is less inflationary than the outright creation of new money.

items.value: Increase in the banking habit of the people
items.reasoning: The money multiplier falls as either the reserve ratio or the currency-to-deposit ratio rises. When people bank more of their money instead of holding cash, the currency-deposit ratio drops, more of every rupee stays in the banking system available for onward lending, and the multiplier rises — so C is correct. Raising the CRR (A) or the SLR (B) locks up a larger share of deposits and shrinks the multiplier. Population size (D) has no bearing on the ratios that determine it.

items.value: Expansionary policies, fiscal stimulus and higher purchasing power only — indexed wages and rising interest rates are not demand-pull causes
items.reasoning: Demand-pull inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods', so anything that lifts aggregate demand qualifies: expansionary monetary and fiscal policy (1), fiscal stimulus (2) and higher purchasing power (4) all do. Statement 5 is decisive against the other options — rising interest rates are contractionary, raising the cost of borrowing and dampening consumption and investment, so they cannot cause demand-pull inflation. Since 5 appears in options B, C and D, all three are excluded, leaving A. Statement 3 is correctly left out as well: inflation-indexed wages belong to the cost-push side, propagating an existing price rise through a wage-price spiral rather than originating an excess of demand.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 only — retail investors can access the G-sec primary market and NDS-OM is the RBI's trading platform; CDSL is not promoted by the RBI
items.reasoning: Statement 3 is false and settles the question: the Central Depository Services Ltd was promoted by the Bombay Stock Exchange along with several commercial banks, not by the Reserve Bank of India — the RBI promotes no depository. That removes options C and D. Statement 2 is correct: NDS-OM is the RBI's anonymous, screen-based order-matching platform for trading government securities. Statement 1 is also correct — retail investors can bid in the primary market for Treasury Bills and dated government securities under the non-competitive bidding facility, holding them in a demat account.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — WaterCredit applies microfinance to water and sanitation and seeks to end dependence on subsidies, but it is not a WHO/World Bank initiative
items.reasoning: WaterCredit is an initiative of the non-governmental organisation Water.org, which extends small affordable loans through microfinance institutions so that poor households can pay the up-front cost of a tap connection or a toilet — so statement 1 is correct, and statement 3 captures its stated purpose of replacing charity and subsidy with credit that the borrower repays. Statement 2 is wrong on the sponsorship: it was neither launched by nor operates under the aegis of the World Health Organization and the World Bank, which knocks out options A, B and D.

items.value: Statement 2 only — providing liquidity to banks facing a temporary crisis
items.reasoning: The lender-of-last-resort function is a banking-system function: the central bank stands ready to lend to a solvent bank suffering a temporary liquidity shortage, so that a run on one institution does not cascade into a systemic collapse. Statement 1 is wrong because the RBI does not lend directly to trade and industry bodies at all. Statement 3 describes a different facility altogether — advances to government to bridge temporary mismatches are Ways and Means Advances, and financing budget deficits is deficit financing, neither of which is the lender-of-last-resort role.

items.value: Environmentally responsible practices in the electronics recycling industry
items.reasoning: R2 stands for 'Responsible Recycling'. The R2 Code of Practices is the certification standard for electronics recyclers and refurbishers, setting requirements on data security, worker health and safety, and the downstream tracking of e-waste so that discarded electronics are not dumped or exported irresponsibly. It has nothing to do with Ramsar wetlands (B), with cultivating degraded land (C), or with the Environmental Impact Assessment process (D).

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 only — heavy-metal leaching from copper slag and sulphur dioxide emissions; lethal carbon monoxide release is not the concern
items.reasoning: Copper is smelted from sulphide ores, so roasting and smelting drive off large volumes of sulphur dioxide — the pollutant at the centre of every controversy over copper smelters, making statement 3 correct. Statement 2 is also correct: the slag left behind carries residual copper, lead, arsenic and cadmium, which can leach out into soil and groundwater when it is dumped or used as fill. Statement 1 is the odd one out — carbon monoxide is a hazard of carbon-reduction processes such as iron and steel blast furnaces, and copper smelters are not known for releasing lethal quantities of it into the environment.

items.value: All three — furnace oil is a refinery product, is used by industry to generate power, and its combustion emits sulphur
items.reasoning: Furnace oil is a heavy residual fuel oil drawn from the bottom of the crude distillation column, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is correct because industries burn it in boilers and captive generating sets for process heat and power, particularly where grid supply is unreliable. Statement 3 follows from its chemistry: being a residual fraction it retains a high sulphur content, and burning it releases sulphur dioxide — which is precisely why its industrial use has been restricted in and around several Indian cities.

items.value: Carbon captured by oceans and coastal ecosystems
items.reasoning: Blue carbon is the carbon stored by marine and coastal ecosystems — chiefly mangroves, tidal salt marshes and seagrass meadows, along with the open ocean — and it is significant because these systems lock carbon into waterlogged sediments where it can remain for centuries. Carbon in forests and farm soils (B) is 'green carbon'; carbon in fossil fuels (C) and in the atmosphere (D) are not sequestration terms at all.

items.value: Lichen and moss
items.reasoning: Lichens are the classic pioneers of bare rock: the fungal partner grips the surface while the algal partner photosynthesises, and the pair draws water and minerals directly from rain and the rock face, needing no soil at all. Mosses are non-vascular and rootless, absorbing water and nutrients over their whole surface through rhizoids that merely anchor them, so they too colonise bare rock, walls and tree bark. Ferns are vascular plants with true roots and normally require a soil substrate, and mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of fungi that must draw nutrients from an organic substrate — which is why options A and D fail. The judgement call is between 'lichen only' and 'lichen and moss'; moss is genuinely found on soil-free surfaces, so C is preferred, but that is the reason for MED rather than HIGH.

items.value: Lemongrass
items.reasoning: Lemongrass (Cymbopogon species) yields citronella oil, whose citral and citronellal content masks the human scent cues mosquitoes track — it is the standard botanical source of natural mosquito repellents. Congress grass (Parthenium) is an invasive weed causing dermatitis and asthma, elephant grass is a fodder and biomass crop, and nut grass (Cyperus rotundus) is a troublesome agricultural weed; none is used as a repellent.

items.value: Cyanobacteria and diatoms
items.reasoning: Primary producers must fix carbon themselves. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes and diatoms are photosynthetic single-celled algae; together they form the bulk of ocean phytoplankton and the base of the marine food chain, so 2 and 3 are correct. Copepods are small crustaceans — zooplankton that graze on phytoplankton, hence consumers, not producers. Foraminifera are heterotrophic shelled protists that feed on algae and detritus, so they too sit above the producer level.

items.value: Hedgehog and pangolin
items.reasoning: The hedgehog curls into a tight ball so that its spine-covered back faces outward and its soft face and belly are enclosed. The pangolin does exactly the same with its overlapping keratin scales — the behaviour is the origin of its name, from a Malay word meaning 'one that rolls up'. The marmot has no such defence: it is a large burrowing ground squirrel that escapes predators by whistling an alarm call and bolting down its burrow, so statement 2 is wrong and only option D fits.

items.value: Statements 1, 2 and 4 — endorsed at the 2014 UN Climate Summit, it sets a global timeline to end forest loss and is endorsed by governments, companies and indigenous communities; it is voluntary and India did not sign at inception
items.reasoning: The New York Declaration on Forests was launched and first endorsed at the UN Climate Summit in New York in September 2014 (statement 1), and it sets out dated goals — halving the loss of natural forests by 2020 and striving to end it by 2030 — which is the global timeline of statement 2. Its endorsers span national and sub-national governments, multinational companies, indigenous peoples' organisations and NGOs, so statement 4 is correct. Statement 3 is false: it is an explicitly voluntary, non-legally-binding political declaration. Statement 5 is also false — India was not among the endorsers at its inception. Since every option other than A carries statement 3 or statement 5, A is the only consistent choice.

items.value: Brakes of motor vehicles, engines of motor vehicles and power plants only
items.reasoning: Magnetite nanoparticles of the kind found in brain tissue are combustion- and friction-derived. Brake pads abrading against discs shed iron-oxide particles (1), high-temperature combustion in vehicle engines produces them in exhaust (2), and coal-burning power plants emit them in fly ash (4). Microwave ovens (3) heat food by dielectric absorption and emit no particulate matter at all, and telephone lines (5) are passive conductors carrying no combustion or wear process, so both are excluded — leaving option B.
